reason: The sources provide dozens of corroborated technical and historical facts across multiple distinct sites detailing Buran's automated orbital flight and subsequent demise.
story: During the Cold War, Soviet military leaders feared NASA's Space Shuttle could dive from orbit to drop nuclear bombs on Moscow. In response, the USSR spent billions building its own shuttle: Buran. Although it looked nearly identical to NASA's orbiter on the outside, Buran was radically different under the skin. It carried no heavy main launch engines, relying instead on the monster Energia rocket. On November 15, 1988, Buran launched on its maiden voyage with no crew aboard. With the cockpit empty and displays dark, its onboard computer handled the entire mission. Buran orbited Earth twice, executed an automated re-entry, and battled fierce 30-plus mile-per-hour crosswinds to touch down on a Baikonur runway just meters from the centerline. It was the first spaceplane in history to fly and land completely on autopilot. Yet Buran never flew again, and was ultimately crushed when its hangar collapsed in 2002.
angle: In 1988, the Soviet Union launched an uncrewed clone of the Space Shuttle that flew to orbit and made a pinpoint runway landing entirely on autopilot—a feat NASA's shuttle never matched.

claims.claim: Buran translates to 'snowstorm' or 'blizzard' in Russian.
The Soviet Buran programme was authorized and formally begun in 1976.
The program was created directly in response to the United States Space Shuttle program.
Soviet leadership feared the American Space Shuttle could execute surprise atmospheric dives to deliver nuclear weapons.
Soviet intelligence and the KGB collected American shuttle technical documentation and research data during development.
Construction of the Buran orbiters began in 1980.
The first suborbital test flight of a scale model occurred in July 1983.
The first full-scale orbiter airframe was rolled out in 1984.
The jet-powered aerodynamic test article OK-GLI flew 24 test flights before being retired.
Buran made its only orbital flight on November 15, 1988.
Buran launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome at 03:00 UTC.
The orbiter was boosted into space by the super-heavy Energia rocket.
Unlike the US Space Shuttle, Buran carried no main launch engines on the orbiter itself.
The maiden orbital flight was entirely uncrewed, with no human pilots on board.
Buran circled the Earth twice during its orbital mission.
The spacecraft performed a fully automatic runway landing under computer control.
Buran touched down on the runway despite strong crosswinds exceeding 30 miles per hour.
The Buran program was officially canceled in 1993 by Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
On May 12, 2002, the flight orbiter Buran was destroyed when the roof of Building 112 collapsed at Baikonur.
The 2002 hangar collapse killed eight workers.

disputed: Crosswind speed during landing: S1 records 61.2 km/h (38.0 mph) while S3 records 34 mph. The script should attribute generally: 'battling howling crosswinds of over thirty miles per hour'.

Missing thermal tiles: S1 reports eight tiles were lost out of 38,000, whereas S3 states only five were missing. The script should attribute as 'between five and eight tiles lost' or omit the exact count.

Casualty breakdown of the 2002 collapse: S1 specifies six workers confirmed dead and two presumed dead (plus a later heart failure death), while S2 and S5 state eight workers were killed. The script should cite 'eight workers lost their lives'.
